title: Unordered List
description: The ul element for bulleted, order-independent content like navigation and features.
subject: html
html:
The <ul> element creates a bulleted list — used when items are related but their order carries no real meaning.

Syntax

<ul>
    <li>First item</li>
    <li>Second item</li>
</ul>

Basic Example

<h2>What's Included</h2>
<ul>
    <li>Live doubt-solving sessions</li>
    <li>Downloadable notes</li>
    <li>Certificate of completion</li>
</ul>

Browser output: three bullet points — reordering these three items wouldn't change what the list actually communicates, which is exactly what makes <ul> the correct choice here.

How It Works

Every direct <li> child gets a bullet marker from the browser's default stylesheet. Unlike <ol>, there's no built-in numbering logic — just a repeated marker.

Important Attributes

AttributePurpose
— none special —Bullet style is controlled via CSS list-style-type, not an HTML attribute

Real-World Example

<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/cources">Courses</a></li>
        <li><a href="/notes">Notes</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

Site navigation is one of the most common real-world <ul> use cases — the visual bullets are usually removed with CSS, but the semantic list structure remains valuable for screen readers regardless.

Comparison: ol vs ul (quick recap)

Use <ol> when sequence is part of the content's meaning; use <ul> when it isn't. Full table: ordered-list.

Common Mistakes

  • Using a <ul> for content that's actually sequential (steps, rankings) — that belongs in <ol>
  • Building a "list" out of multiple <p> tags each starting with a manually typed dash or bullet character

Best Practices

  • Use real <ul>/<li> markup for any group of related, order-independent items
  • Style bullets (or remove them entirely, as in navigation menus) with CSS — never fake or hide them with manual characters

Accessibility Considerations

Removing bullets visually with CSS (common for nav menus) doesn't remove the semantic list structure underneath — screen readers still correctly announce it as a list, which is exactly the point of using real markup even when it isn't styled to look like one.

SEO Considerations

Genuine list markup helps search engines parse grouped content like feature lists or ingredient lists, and can contribute to rich result eligibility.

Browser & Modern HTML Notes

Stable and unchanged across HTML versions — one of the most universally supported elements in the language.

Mini Practice

  1. Build an unordered list of 4 features for a hypothetical app.
  2. Style a navigation <ul> to remove its bullets with CSS, while keeping the underlying list markup.
